title: White House Budget Proposes Eliminating LSC, Defunding Civil Legal Aid for Millions of Low-Income Americans
author: Legal Services Corporation

dom.t: LSC funding: Preservation came with reduced resources

st.t: LSC funding: Preservation came with reduced resources
st.an: The source supports preserving federal civil legal-aid funding and argues that elimination or inadequate funding would sharply reduce service capacity. It also aligns with the synthesis by treating these effects as conditional forecasts tied to proposed cuts, not evidence of consequences from the final $540 million appropriation.
qs: If this budget is approved, LSC-funded aid would disappear for everyday Americans facing urgent civil legal problems like evictions, foreclosures, domestic violence, fraud, consumer scams, and predatory or medical debt.

Without sufficient funding, legal aid providers will be forced to shrink their programs, reduce staff, shutter branch offices, close legal resource clinics and turn away an increasing number of eligible clients with significant legal problems.

kp.k: FY 2026 budget proposes eliminating federal civil-aid funder
kp.d: The May 30, 2025 LSC press release reports that President Trump’s FY 2026 budget proposes eliminating LSC, allocating just $21 million for close-out costs compared with its $560 million FY 2025 Congressional appropriation, which maintained FY 2024 funding. Elimination is a proposal conditional on budget approval, not an enacted outcome. The document addresses civil legal aid funding and access to justice, not AI.
qs: For FY 2026, the Trump Administration has proposed that LSC receive just $21 million for close-out costs.
In FY 2025, LSC received a Congressional appropriation of $560 million through the Continuing Resolution signed by President Trump.
This was flat funding based on the FY 2024 appropriation for the federal government.

kp.k: Proposed defunding threatens nationwide legal-aid provision
kp.d: LSC describes itself as the nation’s single largest civil legal aid funder and reports supporting services for more than five million low-income Americans annually, including more than a million children, over 200,000 domestic violence survivors and nearly 45,000 veterans. The body identifies 130 funded providers with over 900 offices serving every county, the District of Columbia and U.S. territories; the closing description instead gives 129 independent nonprofit programs, without reconciling the counts.
qs: LSC is the nation’s single largest funder of civil legal aid.
Currently, LSC funds support legal services for more than five million low-income Americans annually.
This includes more than a million children, over 200,000 survivors of domestic violence and nearly 45,000 veterans.
Defunding LSC would strip grant funding that supports 130 legal aid providers with over 900 offices in every county of every state, as well as the District of Columbia and the U.S. territories.
The Corporation currently provides funding to 129 independent nonprofit legal aid programs in every state, the District of Columbia, and U.S. territories.

kp.k: LSC predicts staffing cuts and reduced client access
kp.d: The release predicts that inadequate funding would force providers to reduce programs and staffing, close offices and clinics, and reject more eligible clients. It links these anticipated capacity losses to urgent civil problems involving housing, income, healthcare, child custody and protection from abuse. These are LSC’s prospective warnings rather than reported effects of an implemented cut.
qs: Without sufficient funding, legal aid providers will be forced to shrink their programs, reduce staff, shutter branch offices, close legal resource clinics and turn away an increasing number of eligible clients with significant legal problems.

These LSC-funded legal aid organizations do vital work assisting low-income people who are facing urgent civil legal problems that could cause them to lose their home, income, healthcare, custody of their children or an order of protection from an abuser.

kp.k: Lawyer-dependent justice system leaves low-income people vulnerable
kp.d: LSC President Ron Flagg argues that a justice system built for lawyers often leaves people unable to access justice when they cannot afford counsel, referring to 52 million Americans qualifying for LSC-funded services. The release states that eligibility covers household incomes at or below 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines and that sixteen percent of Americans currently qualify. Eligibility figures are distinct from the annual service figures.
qs: “Because our justice system was built for lawyers, it is too often true that there is no hope of accessing justice when legal problems arise for the 52 million Americans who qualify for LSC-funded services and have no means to afford an attorney,” Flagg continued.
Individuals who have a household income at or below 125% of the Federal Poverty Guidelines are eligible for LSC-funded legal assistance.
Sixteen percent of Americans currently qualify.

kp.k: LSC reports sevenfold average return on civil legal aid
kp.d: The release reports that LSC’s analysis of over 50 studies found an average return of $7 for every $1 invested in civil legal aid. It attributes economic benefits to preventing or resolving problems that generate emergency medical, law-enforcement and shelter expenditures, alongside greater family stability, participation in local economies and reduced reliance on assistance. The release does not supply individual study details or methods.

The brief demonstrates the positive economic impact that civil legal aid creates by preventing and solving legal problems that lead to costly public expenditures on things like emergency medical care, law enforcement and shelters.
Legal aid also helps improve family stability, leading to increased participation in local economies and reduced reliance on other forms of assistance.

kp.k: Bipartisan legal stakeholders call for robust LSC funding
kp.d: The release reports FY 2026 funding appeals from leaders of 160 U.S. law firms, 40 bipartisan state attorneys general and 37 bipartisan state supreme court chief justices. It situates these appeals alongside LSC’s Congressional establishment in 1974 and bipartisan governance, noting that most current board members were appointed during President Trump’s first term. The funding recommendation is attributed to the external stakeholders.
qs: Recent letters from external stakeholders have called for Congress to provide robust funding for LSC in FY 2026.
LSC is governed by a bipartisan Board of Directors, appointed by the President and confirmed by the Senate.
By law, LSC’s Board is comprised of roughly equal numbers of Republicans and Democrats, with the majority representing the current Administration.

pts.k: The source makes no claims or predictions about AI.
pts.d: This LSC press release concerns the proposed elimination of federal funding for civil legal aid in FY 2026 and its anticipated effects on providers and low-income Americans. It does not discuss AI or attribute changes in legal services to AI. Its funding-related claims therefore do not supply evidence, timeframes or affected populations for an AI-related claim.
